title: It was Brahman
hookLine: Uma answers: it was Brahman, the victory was never yours, and Brahman is to be loved as the dear one
carry: brahman is the dear one behind every power
tomorrow: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (1 of 7)

cards: Sometimes the truth about a thing only arrives afterward. A grown woman learns that a teacher quietly paid her school fees. A son learns that his parents skipped meals so he could eat.
Every memory of those years rearranges itself: oh. It was you, all along. Indra is standing in empty space beside a radiant woman, and he asks her what that wondrous being was.
Her answer rearranges the whole story.

teach.b: Section four. Uma says: it is Brahman. It was in Brahman's victory that you were glorying.
And then Indra knew. That's the whole reveal. The victory the gods called ours was Brahman's.
The fire that could burn and the wind that could carry were Brahman's power, lent.

The text adds that Agni, Vayu and Indra stand above the other gods because they came nearest to it, and Indra above them all, because he was the first to know it was Brahman. Then the teaching turns inward.
Like a flash of lightning, like the blink of an eye: ah! It isn't held; it flashes, and you're changed. And in yourself?
The mind moves toward it, and remembers it, again and again.
Then a name to hold onto: tadvanam, which Shankara reads as the one who is adored, the dear one. Meditate on it as the beloved, the text says, and all beings will love such a person.
Finally the student asks: teach me the Upanishad. The teacher says: it's been taught. Its foundation is discipline, self-control and work.

teach.h: BRAHMAN IS THE DEAR ONE BEHIND EVERY POWER.
teach.b: So, the week in one line: the one the mind runs on was behind the victory, all along. And notice how the Kena ends. Not with a cold force to be understood.

With a beloved. Many teachers read it this way: that's how a Hindu can study Brahman in the morning and sing to Krishna or the Mother at night with no contradiction. The ground of everything is also the dear one.

how: In Vedanta study the Kena is read with commentaries such as Shankara's; Uma's answer, 'it is Brahman', marks the moment the gods learn their power was never their own.

o: the far one, beyond all reach
the hidden one, found in forests
the dear one, the one who is adored

games.q: the end of the story — tap the pairs.
p: first to know it was Brahman

s: Uma tells Indra the victory was the gods' own
she says it was Brahman's victory, and they were glorying in it.
the Kena says Brahman is glimpsed like a flash of lightning
like lightning, like the blink of an eye.
the Kena says truth is the home of the teaching
discipline, self-control and work its foundation; the Vedas its limbs; truth its home.

games.q: Indra asks Uma: what was that wondrous being? what does she say?
o: 'it is Brahman; the victory was its, not yours.'
games.why: it is Brahman. in Brahman's victory you were glorying. and then Indra knew.

practice: Pick one moment from this week when something flashed: a sound you really heard, a flinch that softened, a question that opened.

Hold it the way the Kena says the mind holds Brahman, coming back to it again and again, gently, like returning to someone dear. If you pray, end with the name of God you love best, said like the name of a friend.

wordCard.voice: Tadvana, the one who is adored, the dear one. Uma told Indra: it is Brahman; the victory you were glorying in was Brahman's. Meditate on it as the beloved.

orig.note: Sanskrit: tadvana, read by Shankara as the one who is adored, the dear one; Kena 4.6.

carryVoice: Your line: brahman is the dear one behind every power. Tomorrow, a boy walks into the house of Death. The Kena, all seven days, complete.

sources.ref: Kena Upanishad 4.7–4.8 (the foundation of the teaching; truth its home)
